name: Osteocalcin

lead: Osteocalcin is a protein made by bone-building cells, and doctors use its blood level as a marker of how actively bone is forming. Bone-focused readers connect it to bone strength and metabolism.

Since 2007, mouse studies have proposed that it also acts as a hormone on insulin, muscle and testosterone, with the uncarboxylated form signalling through receptors such as GPRC6A and GPR158. Human relevance is still being investigated, and no studies test it for looks.

paras: It is not a marketed product. In practice people encounter it as a blood test of bone formation, and discussion of it centres on supporting the bone and vitamin K pathways that produce it.
No approved therapeutic use or safety data for administering it are described. Human studies reviewed measure it as a marker rather than as a treatment.

social.title: Osteocalcin, hormone produced in bone, may regulate metabolism
Looking for that osteocalcin rush? Skeleton holds the key to “fight or flight”

angle.text: Osteocalcin is a bone-made protein and proposed hormone, and bone-focused readers connect it to stronger bone structure and metabolic benefits. It is studied as a marker of bone formation and, in animals, for effects on insulin and muscle; no looks-related use has been tested in humans.

lead: Osteocalcin (gene BGLAP) is a small, 49-amino-acid protein made by bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) and found in bone and dentin. Its synthesis and calcium binding depend on vitamin K-dependent carboxylation, and its blood level is widely used as a marker of bone formation.[1]

Since 2007 it has also been studied as a possible bone-derived hormone. Experiments in mice reported that the skeleton influences insulin secretion and energy metabolism through the uncarboxylated form of the protein.[2] Researchers have also reported effects on muscle, testosterone production and the brain in animal studies.[1]

Osteocalcin is an endogenous protein rather than a product sold for appearance purposes. The sources reviewed describe no approved therapeutic use and no published trial testing osteocalcin itself as an intervention for looks, body composition or bone growth.

paras: Osteocalcin contains gamma-carboxyglutamate residues, which let it bind calcium and concentrate in bone. It was first reported in developing chick bone by Hauschka and Reid in 1978, and the primary structure of the monkey protein was published in 1982.[1]

Osteoblast differentiation depends on the transcription factor Cbfa1 (also called Osf2), which was first identified through its binding to an element in the osteocalcin promoter.[3][4] Mice lacking osteocalcin showed increased bone formation in a 1996 report.[5]

In 2007 Lee and colleagues reported in Cell that, in mice, uncarboxylated osteocalcin acts on pancreatic beta cells and on fat tissue, linking the skeleton to glucose handling and energy expenditure.[2] Later work summarised by Wikipedia reports proposed roles in muscle exercise capacity, testosterone synthesis in the testes, brain function and the acute stress response, mediated by receptors such as GPRC6A and GPR158.[1]
These findings come mainly from rodent experiments, and the extent to which they apply to humans is still being investigated.
Serum osteocalcin is commonly measured as an indicator of osteoblast activity, for example in studies of anabolic osteoporosis drugs.[1]

No studies found of osteocalcin itself as a treatment for appearance. Registered human studies mostly measure osteocalcin as an outcome or marker, for instance after vitamin K supplementation in adults and children, with vitamin D, or in metformin-treated women with polycystic ovary syndrome.[6][7][8] One registered vitamin K and osteocalcin study in ageing adults was terminated.[7]

timeline.event: Hauschka and Reid report a calcium-binding, gamma-carboxyglutamate-containing protein in chick bone.[1]
Osteocalcin-deficient mice are reported to have increased bone formation.[5]
Lee et al. propose endocrine regulation of energy metabolism by the skeleton via osteocalcin.[2]
